candidates.source_title: Album is still banging the drum for town’s music heritage - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: An album which is believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council has reached millions of listeners on national radio and streaming platforms. Kenion Street has enjoyed glowing reviews after being launched as part of Rochdale’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture. It features local acts performing their version of a classic track originally recorded at iconic studios in the town. From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to both Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios in Kenion Street, where trailblazing artists including OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, Inspiral Carpets, Autechre, A Certain Ratio, The Fall and many others recorded some of their most memorable work. The 11 tracks on Kenion Street included PoolEra’s version of Electricity by OMD, Dreams Never End by New Order re-imagined by Medley, and Jennifer Read’s dramatic version of Totally Wired, by The Fall. Micah Stalgic and choir Local Vocals performing Atmosphere by Joy Division, that features on the album All the new tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, based in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building in Kenion Street, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. Radio 6 Music also featured the album, playing Middleton band’s K-Estate’s version of Gang of Four’s Damaged Goods. It was also made Track of the Day on Radio X with other tracks played across XS Manchester, Mersey Radio, Phoenix FM and many more, with a combined audience of over 3.5 million.

candidates.source_title: New college building reaches construction milestone - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A special topping out ceremony marked a major milestone in the construction of the Clegg Building at Hopwood Hall College. Being built by Willmott Dixon and funded by the Department for Education, Rochdale Council and the college, the landmark development is poised to become a modern and inspiring learning environment in the heart of Rochdale. The building was visited by Principal and CEO Julia Heap OBE, Rochdale Member of Parliament Paul Waugh, the Mayor and Mayoress of Rochdale, Faisal Rana and Iram Faisal, among others. Members of the family of the late Robert Clegg OBE, in whose honour the new building has been named, joined as special guests for the event. Robert served as Chair of the Corporation at Hopwood Hall College from 2007 to 2018, making a significant contribution to the college during his time in the role. Robert’s wife Anne, son Richard and daughter Emma attended the ceremony to mark the occasion, with Emma continuing the family’s connection to the college as a current part-time adult learner. During the ceremony, the team from Willmott Dixon led visitors to the roof of the structure, which offers sweeping views of the borough, including Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Parish Church. There was then an opportunity for visitors to leave a message on part of the roof parapet in what will now become a permanent record of the occasion.

candidates.source_title: Trafford MV slip to third after defeat at Littleborough - Messenger Newspapers
candidates.source_body_excerpt: As storms blew across the country, Trafford MV found themselves in the midst of their own storm at league leaders Littleborough in ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2. Trafford went into the game missing a number of regular players through injury and unavailability, but made good headway in the first half despite the terrible conditions. Mica Dyos opened the scoring following good forward drives playing down the slope for a 5-0 lead. Littleborough forced a penalty in the MV '22' which then resulted in an easy score and conversion for the home side which took them into a half-time lead at 7-5. In the second half, Littleborough made better use of the slope and conditions in front of the dwindling crowd driven under cover by the driving wind and rain. The upper hand was grasped with an early try, followed by a well-kicked penalty to make it 15-7. This was built on with a further try under the posts for 22-7, but a yellow card came for the home hooker. Trafford forced a five-metre scrum from which stand-off Aaron Booth scored and converted to reduce the arrears to 22-12.

candidates.source_title: 34 Rochdale foster families honoured at an awards event in Rochdale Town Hall
candidates.source_body_excerpt: 34 Rochdale foster families, collectively fostering for 465 years, have been honoured at the annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards at Rochdale Town Hall for their dedicated service. Rochdale foster carers have been honoured at Rochdale Town Hall in gratitude for their commitment to providing safe, stable, and nurturing homes for some of the most vulnerable. It is estimated that the carers have supported more than 1020 children and young people from newborn to 18 combined, whilst working with the local authority. Michael (79) and Marilyn (75) were honoured for 50 years of fostering since 1976, working predominantly with newborn babies and siblings. The married couple from Milnrow have cared for over 330 children in those years. Marilyn was asked how long she was to continue to foster for, "How long is a piece of string?" she remarked, before adding that she would really miss fostering. "We’ve been to their weddings, adoption parties, christenings, eighteenth, and twenty first birthday parties. “It’s lovely when you think you started off with them as a baby and now, they’ve grown. “We’ve had letters from adoptive parents saying, ‘They’ve turned out like they have because of you’ which is nice.”

candidates.source_title: Nursery loses bid to keep ‘outbuilding’ caravan - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A nursery has lost its bid to keep a caravan which replaced a temporary Portakabin in its yard. Little Oaks Nursery applied to Rochdale Council for retrospective planning permission for the caravan which is being used as an outbuilding at its site in Bamford Road, Heywood. It follows planning permission granted in 2022 for a temporary Portakabin classroom which was removed in 2024. A planning officer’s report said: “Simultaneously, pre-application advice was requested and given for the siting of a static caravan on the site. “The advice given was that such a structure would not be visually appropriate for the site and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. “Notwithstanding, it appears that a static caravan was nonetheless placed at the site without the benefit of planning permission and this application therefore seeks regulation of such. “The caravan does not provide the high-quality design that officers had previously stated would be required for a permanent structure. “In design terms, the caravan is of no visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaces, which was accepted only for a temporary period on the basis that it was unacceptable for permanent retention.

candidates.source_title: Unseen pictures of 1930s from Manchester's Ritz to Rochdale 'Riviera' - Manchester Evening News
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Storm clouds were gathering again globally. But on Boxing Day 1938 she captured, vivaciously, just one aspect of that decade. Crimson-lipped the cashier of the Ritz Dancing Hall in Manchester reflected the population's determination to find joy after the dark days of the First World War, the Great Depression, and unemployment. The 1930s led novelist and broadcaster JB Priestley to his famous vision of "three Englands" – the ancient country of cathedrals and villages, the blackened and scarred industrial Britain created by the Victorians, and the Americanised new consumer world of suburbs, cinemas and motorcars. He came to the conclusion after travelling the country with his suitcase and a typewriter to find material for his book "English Journey" published in 1934. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The decade in Britain saw a nation in transition. The north was hit hard by economic turmoil with unemployment levels soaring above the national average due to the collapse of industries like coal mining and shipbuilding. However, seaside cities became alive in the 1930s, thanks to the expansion of cheap rail travel and the emerging concept of paid holidays with thousands of working-class families flooding to the coast during their “Wakes Weeks” But the south and the midlands had seen a growth in new industries, notably car making, and electrical goods, and were able to withstand the economic fallout which the book says were distributed in a "grotesquely uneven way". A picture of a young, very well dressed couple, on Oxford Street, London, shows how affluence thrived in parts of the country while elsewhere, like the Lancashire George Orwell (pen name for Eric Blair) discovered in his travelogue "The Road to Wigan Pier" working class communities were decimated by the decline of traditional industries. The land as a place of marked contrasts is captured in a new book, Britain in the 1930s by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill from Atlantic Publishing, price £50. candidates.source_title: No decision yet on College Bank – but ‘renovation would take more than a decade’ - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Renovating Rochdale’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks would force residents out of their homes for more than a decade, housing chiefs have said. While Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says no decision on the future of the landmark College Bank blocks has been taken, residents have asked new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig to back their campaign to refurbish their homes rather than demolish them. But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Members of Greater Manchester Tenants Union recently met Ms Craig to discuss the steps that could be taken to renovate almost 1,000 homes in College Bank and Lower Falinge. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes.

candidates.source_title: The secret safety battle over Rochdale’s Seven Sisters
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Claire Lord sits alone in her living room surrounded by head-high boxes. The small space between her sofa and TV is the only bit of the flat not crowded by cubes of clutter. To answer the door she has to clamber over yet more plastic tubs filled to the brim with her worldly possessions. The 56-year-old is ready to move out of her flat in Rochdale ’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks. She’s been ready for weeks. Claire was one of 229 households told they had to leave by landowners Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) in October 2025. Since then, droves have been moving out of the blocks. Only an estimated 90 households are still left in Seven Sisters - actually named College Bank. RBH says this has been done for safety reasons. The tower blocks face an uncertain future, with the question of demolition or refurbishment still on the table after a decade of limbo. No matter the decision, it is understood all residents will have to move out whilst work is done - whether that work is to decorate or destroy. Claire is one of the latest to be exiting the estate, but it’s not a move she really wanted to do. When describing the day when RBH told her they'd found some new digs for her, she said she was ‘gutted’. The security, the views, proximity to healthcare professionals and the community are the things she cherishes most about her flat. Claire will be moving to a bungalow across the road, behind Lidl. “There has been a delay because the lady who lived in the bungalow hadn't done work on the place for some time,” Claire explained. “They’ve had to do painting and decorating, rewiring, putting new doors on and a fresh kitchen. “So they’ve been getting it ready for me. RBH told me about four months ago that I’d be moving and were waiting for the date. “Every time I’ve gone down they’ve come up with more work and more work to do. I’ve been down every week to ask. “It’s always the same story - ‘something is being done’. I’ve still not got a move-in date, I think I’ll be told about a move-in date in four weeks. “I do love living here. The security is good and there isn’t much chance of you getting burgled. “It’s close to the shops in the town centre, my mental health team is nearby and my GP is just down the road. “But my biggest fear of moving is losing that security. I’ve been here (in Mardyke block) for 12 years and I've never had any trouble, it’s a good community. “If I could stay I would. It’s not good for my mental health. I don’t know whether I’m coming or going. “Being stuck halfway is no good as I just don’t know. They’re just going to plonk a day on me.” Claire has credited RBH with supporting her through the transition. candidates.source_title: Accrington boss John Doolan sets play-off target after historic win at Rochdale - The Herald
candidates.source_body_excerpt: John Doolan challenged rampant Accrington to push for the play-offs after they cruised to the biggest away win in their Football League history at toothless Rochdale. Josh Woods, Charlie Warren, Tyler Walton – with a brace – and substitute Alex Henderson all struck in a dominant 5-0 victory as Stanley made it nine games in a row unbeaten in all competitions. Remarkably, it was also their first away win since February but it took them up to ninth in League Two. Asked if the play-offs were a genuine incentive for Accy, boss Doolan – whose team finished 16th last term – said: “Yeah, it always has been for us. “We say to the players, you’re trying to progress and develop and be better than last year, and last year at one point, round about February, we were six points off the play-offs. “So to be sitting where we are now, one point off the play-offs, is credit to the players.” Doolan savoured the “outstanding” goals Accy scored as he urged them to build on what he felt was “probably” the best performance of his two-and-a-half-year reign. “A result like that just helps build momentum,” he said. “I think we’ve had that for the past eight, nine games now.

Tyler Walton notched a double as on-song Accrington extended their unbeaten run to nine games in all competitions with an emphatic 5-0 win at Rochdale.

The points were all but secured by half-time as John Doolan's side fired home three impressive strikes before the break on the way to their biggest victory since March 2025.

Dale were booed off after a fifth successive match without victory.

Stanley grabbed the lead in the 14th minute when Josh Woods guided in a low effort from 20 yards out after home goalkeeper Sam Waller passed the ball straight to him.

Walton then slipped a lovely pass through for Charlie Warren to lash a low strike in off the post from the edge of the box in the 38th minute.

Walton arced a stunning angled strike over Waller from just inside the box in first-half stoppage time.

The winger doubled his tally in the 51st minute when he knocked in the rebound after Joe Anderson's shot was saved by Waller.

Sub Alex Henderson sealed the rout in the 66th minute by finishing off a brilliant move from 10 yards out.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A six-bedroom HMO could be created above a restaurant in Littleborough. Abdul Ahad has applied to Rochdale Council to convert part of the first and second floors of 15 Todmorden Road in Littleborough from restaurant and storage into a six-bedroom HMO above the Bay of Bengal restaurant. The application is part retrospective as work has already been carried out to create two roof lights and install a window. In supporting documents submitted to the council, Build Design Services said: “The ground floor is occupied by an established restaurant and will remain in its existing use. “The upper floors are currently vacant and were previously used for office and storage purposes. The proposal seeks to bring these underused areas of the building back into productive use as residential accommodation. “The proposed HMO will provide six single-occupancy bedrooms for a maximum of six residents. Four bedrooms and a shared kitchen/living area will be provided at first-floor level, with a further two bedrooms and bathroom facilities at second-floor level. READ MORE: ‘Nobody should face it alone — Sleep Out isn’t about pretending to be homeless’ “The proposal represents the effective reuse of an existing building within the established built-up area of Littleborough. candidates.source_title: Rochdale Council rakes in almost £3m from parking fines
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale council has raked in £2.88m from parking fines in the last three years. Data obtained from a Freedom of Information (FOI) request revealed that the local authority has generated just under £1m per year from 2023 to 2026. From a total of 90,644 parking charge notices (PCNs) issued for 2023, 2024 and 2025, the council gained £2.88m, with the highest earning year being 2025 with £990,256. The total value of PCNs was just over £5.6m, but the income is less due to people successfully challenging claims or costs of chasing fines. The town hall says all money generated from PCNs is then reinvested into the road network. This reinvestment could include fixing potholes, re-drawing on road markers or larger infrastructure projects. The local authority also pointed out PCNs are issued for safety reasons, such as making sure pavements have enough space for wheelchair users or to prevent blind spots at junctions. The FOI, submitted by the Local Democracy Reporting Service, also revealed the biggest hotspots in the borough where people get PCNs. Newgate, Yorkshire Street Central and Oldham Road Central were all the places with the highest number of PCNs distributed. Newgate: Number of PCNs – 790, total income: £54,920 Yorkshire St Central: Number of PCNs – 623, total income: £39,970

candidates.source_title: The scheme to regenerate land around Rochdale station progressing
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say. Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community.
candidates.source_summary: A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say.

candidates.source_title: The potential return of Lodge Mill
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill.

candidates.source_title: Major Rochdale housing scheme delayed again over flood concerns
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The decision over the first phase of a 450-home development in Rochdale has been delayed again. In August, Rochdale council ’s planning committee deferred making a decision on Wain Homes’ proposals to build 45 houses on a plot of land behind Greenvale in Bamford. Committee members felt they didn’t have enough detail about how the developers would solve historic drainage issues. Councillors said the lack of a masterplan for the wider scheme prevented them from making a call. The proposal would be the first of many for the former green belt land, which contains a number of playing fields and sports pitches. The site was taken out of the green belt following the adoption of the Greater Manchester housing strategy, Places for Everyone. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter A new clubhouse for Bridge FC and revamped sports pitches at the site are seen as the major benefits that would come from the overarching scheme. candidates.source_title: Drivers have vehicles seized for ignoring school crossing patrols - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Two drivers have had their vehicles seized after failing to stop for school crossing patrols and almost knocking them over. Rochdale Council has revealed that the incidents — involving a car and a moped — were among 137 incidents in the past five years in which motorists failed to stop for school crossing patrols, as required by law. The incidents took place on October 13 and 14, with school crossing patrol Barry Jones having to move out of the way to avoid the vehicles, even though he was already standing in the road. The matter was reported to police, who used new powers under section 59 of the police reform act 2002, to seize the vehicles after collecting evidence, including witness statements. Cars and other vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols is a growing problem, with 137 fail to stops reported across Rochdale borough over the past five years. Body-worn cameras are now being used in hotspot areas to try to deter dangerous driving and support prosecutions where needed. Cllr Dylan Williams, cabinet member for highways and facilities, said: “It beggars belief that somebody would see a school crossing patrol clearly standing in the middle of the road and continue to drive. Frankly I’m appalled. “We would like to thank GMP for their quick and decisive action and I think it’s a really good result.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale town centre has won gold and been named the Town Centres and City Centres category winner at the 2026 Britain in Bloom awards. They also recognised work to support biodiversity and partnerships between volunteers, businesses and council teams. The entry included the restored Grade I listed Rochdale Town Hall, the new Town Hall Square and improvements to the Broadfield Park slopes. The restoration and surrounding improvements received support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. The Baillie Street Quarter and murals created through the 2025 Rochdale Common Walls Festival also formed part of the town centre’s entry. Councillor Tricia Ayrton, Rochdale Borough Council’s deputy leader and cabinet member for climate change and environment, thanked those involved.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Work can now begin on an £11.4 million new school designed for pupils with special educational needs. Planning permission has been granted for Rochdale Council to create a 64-place alternative provision school on lane off Mayfield Street in Rochdale, as a satellite site for Redwood School for children with complex autism and social-emotional needs related to autism. Work is due to start next year and the school — a Raise Rochdale Pupil Referral School — is due to open September 1, 2028. The vacant former farmland will see a part one, two and three-storey split-level school created, including parking, play areas and landscaping. In documents submitted with the planning application, Seven Architecture said: “This development will deliver a specialist educational facility for pupils aged 11-16 with social, emotional and mental health needs — supporting the council’s objective to expand high-quality SEN provision within the borough. “The proposed scheme will provide accommodation for up to 64 pupils, creating a cafe, secure and therapeutically informed learning environment designed to support vulnerable young people. “The development seeks to deliver a high-quality educational setting that enables staff to effectively manage behaviour, support personal development and deliver specialist teaching within a carefully planned and supportive environment.
